          Across all 92 held-back days, on the booked codes

          Fixed on the first visit?

          86.4%

          from 69.6% sending the nearest technician on today's stock

          Cost a call?

          $93.21

          from $122.08: minutes at $1, second visits at $165, both made up

          Jobs the truck covers?

          90.3%

          from 78.6%, at $109 a truck-day against $180

          Customer's words read right?

          92.6%

          agreement with the booked code, against 48.2% for keyword rules

          Who takes the call

          Every held-back day replayed with the same made-up sick calls, breakdowns and priority changes. Staple sends each call to the technician with the lowest expected cost: drive and repair minutes, plus a second visit times the chance that technician's skill or truck fails it, placing first the call with most to lose?. Shuffling the technicians' skills drops it to 83.3%, below the parts-only rule's 84.1%, so the gain comes from knowing who is good at what. Calls moved by a sick day or a breakdown were fixed first time 77.3% of the time, against 71.2% for the current way. A rolled call? counts as not fixed.

          What a fleet does with this: keep the routing system dispatch already owns, and hand it this expected-cost score for each technician and call, so its routes carry the skill and parts judgment.

          What to load tonight

          Each night the balanced truck ranks every part by its worth? per unit of space. It covers 90.3% of jobs for $109 a truck-day?, against 78.6% and $180 for today's fixed stock, while holding $3,068 against $3,162.

          What a fleet does with this: switch the overnight load from a fixed stock list to tomorrow's booked calls, so the parts room works from a load sheet per truck like the one on the left.

          Claude coding the bookings

          Claude Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5) reads the customer's own words and picks a problem code with a confidence. Asking one question when it is unsure, its 3-part list covers 69.9% of jobs, against 71.6% for the booked code? and 50.4% for keyword rules. So Claude codes a booking about as well as a call-taker, and far better than keyword rules. Random replies to its question drop it to 66.2%, and shuffling its answers between bookings to 32.7%. The answers are saved with the code, so these pages rebuild without a key.

          What a fleet does with this: let Claude code the bookings and ask its one question at the moment of booking, and keep a person on the few calls its question cannot settle.

          Back-orders to chase first

          For each back-ordered part?, the list forecasts the calls that will need it before it arrives, from training history only, and how many have no truck nearby holding one. Over the held-back months it expected 84 calls and 14 stuck; the days then brought 90 and 20.

          What a fleet does with this: expedite from the top of this list, and move spares toward the zones where no truck holds one.

          Which parts to carry

          The predictor ranks parts by how often they fixed the same model family and problem, and leans? on the wider appliance group when a family's history is thin. Three parts on the carry list? cover 71.6% of held-back jobs; the national top three cover 40.3%. Shuffling the history drops the predictor to 38.5%.

          What a fleet does with this: rank each booked call's parts by model family and problem rather than by national usage, and feed those lists to the overnight load.

          Where repeat visits come from

          On today's trucks, a missing part causes 67% of repeat visits?. Washers are worst: 29 of every 100 washer jobs need a second visit because a part was not on board.

          What a fleet does with this: start the pilot on washers, where a missing part costs the most second visits.

          How a fleet would adopt it

          1. Back-test on its own history. The same replay on real calls, parts and technicians, before any truck changes. If the gains vanish there, it stops here.
          2. Pilot one region. Load and dispatch one region by this plan for six weeks against a matched region left as it is, and compare first-visit fix, parts-caused repeat visits and stock value.
          3. Roll out region by region. Each region goes live only after the one before it beat its match.

          What this shows, and what it does not

          The plan on the left runs on Claude's codes for one invented week. The evidence above runs on the call-taker's booked codes for all 92 held-back days, so it measures the planning apart from the reading. Every result reproduces from one seed, and each gain has a shuffled control that falls back when the history's links are broken. None of it shows the gains on a real fleet, because the history is invented. Three corners are cut on purpose: counting instead of a trained model, zone-to-zone drive times instead of road routing, and a call-by-call night plan instead of a solver.
